To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

transplanted rhesus monkey autologous iPSC-derived neural cells survive for up to six months and differentiate into mature neurons, astrocyte and myelinating cells in the brains of hemiparkinsonism monkeys with a minimal inflammatory reaction.

autologous rPSC-derived neural progenitor cells can survive for up to six months and differentiate into multiple cell types in the brains of rhesus monkeys, which is the first report of iPSCs in nonhuman primates.
transplanted neural stem cells from rhesus monkeys survive for 6 months after transplantation and differentiate into neurons and glial cells in the brains of rhesus monkeys.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a cell replacement therapy for Parkinson’s Disease.

understanding and developing the molecular and cellular basis of neural regeneration in the adult brain, with particular emphasis on neural stem/progenitor cells and their progeny, as they relate to the treatment of Parkinson’s disease and other brain disorders.

the use of iPSCs for the generation of neural progenitor cells (NPCs) and the transplantation of NPCs into the brains of nonhuman primates to evaluate the potential of these cells to survive, migrate, and integrate into the host brain.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the transplantation of autologous rPSCs-derived neural cells into a MPTP-induced Parkinsonian rhesus monkey model is safe and that the transplanted cells survive and differentiate into neural cell types.
the iPSC-derived neural cells survive, differentiate, and mature in the monkey brain.

the transplantation of rhesus monkey iPS-derived neural progenitor cells into the brain of MPTP-treated rhesus monkeys results in long-term survival of the grafted cells and the formation of neurons, astrocyte, and oligodendroglia.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we generated iPSCs from a monkey and differentiated them into neural cells.
we generated iPSCs from rhesus monkey fibroblasts, induced them to become neural cells, and then transplanted them into the brains of monkeys with Parkinson's disease.

the autologous rPSC-derived neural progenitor cells survive in the brain of MPTP-treated rhesus monkeys and differentiate into mature neurons, astrocyte, and oligodendroglia, and that the transplanted cells do not induce an inflammatory response in the host brain.
The main takeaway from our work is that
human neural progenitors derived from autologous human iPSCs are capable of surviving, differentiating, and integrating into the nonhuman primes brain for at least 6 months.
iPSC-derived neural cells can be transplanted into the brains of nonhuman primates and that they can survive and mature in vivo for up to 1 year.
iPSC-derived neural cells can survive and differentiate in the nonhuman monkey brain and may be a promising cell source for future regenerative therapies.
